This feels like a refinement of the current re-design, it’s quite tasteful in the layout and typography. I’m not sure about the status, it feels a bit intrusive to a degree, particularly with longer statuses. I do see that some individuals would expect the status to be present though. Short statuses work well with the redesign, whilst longer statuses can feel visually intrusive. That being said, it’s not something simple to resolve.

I’d like to see this design at various distances, considering that this is a 2D element in a 3D space where readability is essential. Due to the resolution of VR across a range of headsets, it’s essential that key identifiable elements like name and avatar remain clearly visible. You may have some trouble with the font that you’ve picked there. You may want to increase the weight of the font as at a distance, as it may start to flicker. The avatar is also something that’s clearly visible and holds essential weight within the design, which is important considering it’s typically one of the most identifiable aspects at a distance.

The golden name for friends is a VRC classic, and for good reason, it’s arguably one of the easiest things to identify at a distance whilst in VR and sets a user apart in a crowd of nameplates. However, it also means that colours like orange, yellow, gold itself, and potentially even light shades of brown could make the text unreadable. 

Considering that users were getting close to the gallows when the gold usernames were removed, it would be advisable to test it with a series of gradients, with having the ‘hero’ gradient colour on the right (e.g. gold) and then towards the left, having a standardised gradient, fading the colour out. I’d recommend experimenting with different types of gradients and more difficult colours, like neon, pastel, and ones closely related to the golden text itself.

Keep in mind that whilst cheap for a singular nameplate, scaled up to 50 or so nameplates, effects typically used within UI design can become computationally expensive. I’d recommend minimising the amount of effects you’re using within the design to maintain performance.

I’d say overall this is a worthwhile improvement to the existing re-design, whilst maintaining the minimalist feel the developers were aiming for, whilst also keeping monetisation elements clearly identifiable but non-intrusive. It is significantly better than many of the other UI mockups that I’ve seen by other individuals. Nicely done.

Ah yes, that’s completely understandable.

If you’re okay with using them, you could use an LLM to have it whip up an emulator in WebGL for you. You can then export the design mockup as an SVG, and have it be displayed at a variety of distances. You can then add things like the infamous screen door effect (for certain headsets), different resolutions, adding a slight blur, etc. You’re also able to add a variety of backgrounds to test readability against them to see how your design performs

If you really want to go all out, you could have it where it supports WebXR, but this is additional work and not really necessary for the design process, a simulated environment is enough to work from and attain valuable feedback. 

That being said, keep in mind of FOV of your emulated camera, it’s hard to quantifiably come up with a solution for what your emulated camera FOV should be, but in general, objects will appear larger than they actually are.

It would not be 1:1 to Unity, but it would provide a valuable simulator of what it may look like in a VR environment.
